content: 1. The concept of supremacy of the artery played a pivotal role in the acquittal of Morikubo, which significantly influenced the trajectory of the chiropractic profession. Following this victory, chiropractic began to market itself as a science, an art, and a philosophy. B.J. Palmer emerged as the Philosopher of Chiropractic. 2. Over the next 15 years, 30 additional chiropractic schools were established, including John Howard's National School of Chiropractic, which later became the National University of Health Sciences and relocated to Chicago, Illinois. Each school sought to establish its unique identity, while B.J. Palmer continued to refine the philosophy underpinning his father’s discoveries. 3. Recent chiropractic graduates, driven by aggressive and provocative advertising, faced immediate arrests by local medical communities wielding state authority. Despite there being only 12,000 practicing chiropractors, over 15,000 prosecutions for practicing medicine without a license occurred within the first 30 years of chiropractic's existence. 4. Tom Moore and Fred Hartwell, through the Universal Chiropractic Association (UCA), successfully defended 80% of these cases. B.J. Palmer later reflected on these legal battles, which deepened the divide between mixers (those combining chiropractic with other treatments) and straights (those practicing pure chiropractic). 5. While B.J. Palmer worked to protect and expand chiropractic through the Palmer School, D.D. Palmer continued to develop his techniques in Oregon. In 1910, D.D. Palmer proposed that nerves control health. Before his sudden and controversial death in 1913, he frequently expressed concerns about B.J. Palmer's management of chiropractic, challenging his methods and philosophy while attempting to regain control of the profession. 6. D.D. Palmer rejected his earlier theory that vertebral subluxations caused pinched nerves in intervertebral spaces. Instead, he proposed that subluxations altered nerve vibrations, either increasing or decreasing tension, which affected the tone (health) of the end organ. 7. State laws to regulate and protect chiropractic practice were eventually introduced in all 50 U.S. states, but the process was fraught with challenges. Medical examining boards sought to maintain control over all healthcare practices, while internal disagreements among chiropractors on how to structure these laws further complicated the effort. 8. Initially, the UCA, led by B.J. When the UCA eventually conceded, B.J. insisted that examining boards consist solely of chiropractors (not mixers) and that educational standards align with those of the Palmer School. 9. In 1922, a Model Bill was drafted to present to states without chiropractic laws. The UCA began a campaign to clean house by warning state associations to expel mixers or face competition from new straight associations. This led to the formation of the American Chiropractic Association (ACA) by mixers, who sought to advance chiropractic education and research. 10. The ACA's growth was initially hindered by its recognition of physiotherapy and other modalities as part of chiropractic. However, its second president, Frank R. Margetts, D.C., supported by the National Chiropractic College, helped the ACA grow by ensuring that college administrators could not hold official positions in the association, giving practicing doctors a collective voice. 11. A disagreement within the UCA in 1924 shifted momentum toward the ACA. B.J. Palmer, still intent on purging mixers, saw the invention of the Neurocalometer (NCM) by Dossa D. Evans as a solution to the legal and financial challenges facing straight chiropractic, particularly the Palmer School. 12. B.J. Palmer, owning the patent for the NCM, planned to limit its distribution to 5,000 units, leasing them exclusively to graduates of Palmer-related schools who were UCA members. He claimed the NCM was the only accurate method to locate subluxations, effectively excluding over 20,000 mixers from defending their practices. 13. The introduction of the NCM caused an uproar among chiropractors. Even Tom Moore, a long-time ally of B.J. Palmer and UCA president, resigned in protest (though he was later reinstated). B.J. 14. B.J. Palmer went on to form the Chiropractic Health Bureau (now the International Chiropractors Association, ICA) with his staunchest supporters, including Fred Hartwell. Membership in the UCA declined, while the ACA's membership increased. In 1930, the ACA and UCA merged to form the National Chiropractic Association (NCA). 15. The NCA established a Committee on Educational Standards (CES), led by John J. Nugent, D.C., to raise educational standards for the profession. Nugent's efforts to consolidate or close substandard schools earned him the nickname Chiropractic's Abraham Flexner from supporters and Chiropractic's Antichrist from detractors. 16. The CES evolved into today’s Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE), which was recognized as the accrediting body for chiropractic by the U.S. Department of Education. Nugent also played a key role in the Chiropractic Research Foundation (now the Foundation for Chiropractic Education and Research, FCER). 17. Differences in state chiropractic laws today can be traced back to these early legal struggles. By the late 1950s, U.S. healthcare had been transformed by medical advancements like penicillin and the polio vaccine. Homeopathic physicians had largely disappeared due to anti-quackery efforts and the leadership of the American Medical Association (AMA). 18. B.J. Palmer reduced chiropractic adjustments to the Hole In One (HIO) technique, focusing solely on the atlas vertebra. Meanwhile, mixers continued to develop and refine proprietary techniques to address subluxations and improve health. 19. Osteopathy in the U.S. evolved alongside medicine, abandoning its reliance on spinal manipulation to treat illness. A similar reform movement began within chiropractic after B.J. Palmer's death in 1961. Samuel Homola, a second-generation chiropractor, advocated for limiting spinal manipulation and proposed that chiropractic focus on conservative care for musculoskeletal conditions. 20. Homola's views echoed those of NCA Chairman C.O. Watkins, D.C., who had warned decades earlier that without scientific validation of chiropractic methods, organized medicine would adopt and integrate valuable techniques into medical practice. Homola's membership in the newly formed ACA was not renewed, and his position was rejected by both straight and mixer associations. 21. In 1975, the National Institutes of Health convened a conference bringing together chiropractors, osteopaths, medical doctors, and Ph.D. scientists to develop strategies for studying the effects of spinal manipulation.
